Do spoon is better than fork to eat spaghetti?

I'm afraid that the conclusion for this one is settled. While certainly there are pastas that can be eaten with a spoon, spaghetti itself has a structure that almost entirely renders a spoon useless as a utensil.

The structure of the spoon and fork are derived from the physics of the materials with which they are intended to interact. Fluids or 'fine' solids that are granular and can flow would simply flow away between the tines of a fork. Contiguous solids are rigid enough that, when pierced, they still hold their shape around the point of incision, thus enabling a piercing implement like a fork to become stuck by way of friction, and so remain manipulable by the utensil--whereas, on a spoon, any imbalance or shift in the center of mass would cause them to simply fall off the spoon.

With regard to spaghetti, while it is not a contiguous solid, friction in its material can cause it to stick together as though solid, and individual strands that are stuck to other strands can become entangled in the fork's tines. With a spoon, however, the spaghetti has limited surface area for friction entanglement, and the center of mass for whatever clump of it that is retrieved from the plate is harder to predict than is appropriate. Using the edge of the spoon to sever the spaghetti to shorter, more simplified strands, would enable one to use a spoon in a pinch... however, extra steps and extra uncertainty count against the spoon while there would be neither with the use of a fork.

I believe for these reasons that the fork is superior to the spoon for the consumption of spaghetti.
And everyone knows you're supposed to use bread to get the rest of the sauce off your plate/bowl. There goes a spoon's only advantage.

Oh my. Between food instability, water shortages, carbon saturation in the atmosphere, oceanic temperatures rising, and bee colonies undergoing colony collapse syndrome by the dozen... We certainly have our work cut out for us.

However, I personally feel as though tackling our carbon problem would lead to solutions in the other areas, especially through re-examining Nuclear Power.

Lots of folks believe that this technology was a dead end ever since the seventies, but my opinion is that we took a wrong turn with it and then gave up prematurely. I admit that focusing our research on reactors that can breed weapons-grade fissile materials was a dumb move. One of the biggest reasons I can accept that is that I know for a fact that this was the debilitating blow that destroyed our capacity to research safer, cleaner, more efficient expressions of this technology for more than forty years.

After both the navy and the army received their nuclear programs, the United States Air Force also was given a little research funding for nuclear. They wanted something absolutely bonkers: A Nuclear Powered Bomber. This was a terrible idea, but when they gave it to Oak Ridge National Labs in Tennessee, it sparked a firestorm of innovation nonetheless. They needed to come up with a reactor that didn't need to be pressurized for the coolant to stay liquid. They needed it to operate at high temperature. They needed it to be chemically inert, as well. Clearly, water-cooling was out of the question, and so was lithium and sodium for the purpose of using liquid metals to cool the reactor since they'd explode in contact with air (especially at high temperatures). So they thought, what are some things that will melt at between 400º and 1500º F, but not get hot enough to melt the pipes if they're made of the right heat-resistant alloys?

And there they came up with the Molten Salt Reactor project.

The MSR design eliminates the problems that eventually came to be the bane of both Chernobyl and Fukushima. Even better, it could operate on an extremely common fissile material--as common in our soil as Lead: Thorium.

Now, to be fair, it wasn't just thorium that it needed. It's that the base 'fuel', Thorium-232, had to be bombarded with neutrons in order to absorb one and become Thorium-233. Thorium-233 has a halflife of about 20 minutes and beta-decays into Protactinium-233. If it accidentally absorbs two neutrons, it'll become Thorium-234 and beta-decay into Protactinium 234, Both of these eventually decay into Uranium-233 or Uranium-234 with a halflife of 27 days or 7 hours respectively. And both of these will readily fission with an expulsion of at least two neutrons (but often up to 3) to fission another Uranium or feed another Thorium a neutron, and release a bunch of energy... this is the cycle that drives the thorium reactor.

The problem is,

It is hard as BALLS to get the Uranium OUT of the reactor at this stage. Separating it from the other materials in the fuel was an arduous process that has insurmountable room for error. And even though it is POSSIBLE to build a weapon with U233,.. well, the US only tested two, and only ONE of them actually worked.

Furthermore, U233 cannot, it just CAN NOT, be turned into Plutonium. It's just not in its decay chain, no matter how many neutrons you throw at it. Because if you throw a neutron at it, it won't absorb; it'll fission, and then it's not uranium anymore. To get Plutonium, you have to start higher on the Uranium isotope chart with U-238.

TL;DR up to this point: we fucked over this elegant, innovative, safe technology because it wasn't dangerous enough.

So why do I think this will solve our carbon problems?

Thorium is more common than coal and it's a waste product of mining rare earth metals. These metals are things we desperately need because their electron orbitals allow us to take advantage of electromagnetic effects we cannot get from anything else. Neodymium, for instance, is why headphones can be earbuds instead of MASSIVE BAKELITE CUPS now--Neodymium Iron Boron magnets are the strongest non-powered magnets to ever exist. We CAN'T mine these ourselves right now though because the NRC demands that Thorium be treated as a 'nuclear waste' even though it has a halflife of almost as long as the age of the universe at just over 14 billion years! Instead, we get all our rare earth materials from CHINA! Fucking CHINA!!! Not only would we get to stop having to burn coal and oil in our power plants, we'd also get to stop shipping this shit from CHINA for a couple thousand barrels of oil every year!

With easy access to rare earth metals, we might see a manufacturing boom, a technology leap, AND all of it on green power. But that's not all!

You see, I'm a proponent of nuclear not only because it generates electricity without emissions, not even radiation unless you blow it the fuck up; no, I think it's great ALSO in that:
a) You don't just turn a nuclear reactor on or off like a switch. They have to be spooled up and spooled down. If it's running at all, it's running. Period. You might as well be using that electricity. Sunk cost fallacy: it's already being wasted if we do nothing.
b) There's a crap ton of waste heat to remove from the system once the heat in question has already done all the turbine spinning that it can.

Why do I like these things?

With all that spare electricity, you can afford to electrolyze water and carbon dioxide to harvest the hydrogen and carbon. And with all that spare electricity, you can also afford to recombine that hydrogen and carbon. Hydrocarbons. AKA, internal combustion fuel. AKA, shit that powers your car! Now, all of a sudden, you are NO LONGER dumping new carbon into the atmosphere! It will have come from the atmosphere in the first place now! This halts the process in its tracks.

With that waste heat... you can desalinate Sea Water by boiling it and collecting the condensate. Cleaner and purer than the clouds themselves! Distillation. Then with all that cheap hydrocarbon internal combustion fuel, you can go ahead and deliver that water anywhere it's needed.

Thermal Depolymerization can furthermore reduce our plastic and organic wastes into a substance not entirely unlike crude oil, the ultimate recycling program.

We can improve the economy, halt carbon emissions, commence carbon harvesting, negate the oil crisis, begin cleaning up our garbage and plastic trash, and have an essentially unlimited supply of clean water to drink or use for agriculture... All just from re-exploring Nuclear with the Molten Salt Thorium Reactor system.
